title: Stop Introducing Your Video. Give People a Reason to Stay.
markdown:
# Stop Introducing Your Video. Give People a Reason to Stay.

At 8:47 p.m., you are trimming the same opening for the fourth time. The video has a useful point. The captions are clean. The cut after the demo lands exactly where it should. Then you watch the first three seconds and hear yourself say, "Today I want to talk about..."

That sentence is doing your viewer no favors. They do not know why the topic matters yet, and their thumb has already moved on.

The opening of a short video has one job: make the right person pause long enough to see the promise proved. It does not need a fake shock or a giant claim. It needs a specific bit of tension that the rest of the video can honestly resolve.

## Start with the moment that hurts

Topics are useful for planning. They are weak openings. "Three ways to plan meals" tells a viewer what folder the video belongs in. "You keep buying groceries for a week and throwing half of them out by Thursday" gives them a reason to care right now.

Look for material with some friction in it: a mistake your audience repeats, a result they cannot get, a belief that costs them time, or a small scene they recognize immediately. The hook should name that moment before it explains the lesson.

For a creator who teaches product photography, these openings do different work:

- "Here are five lighting tips" announces a category.
- "Your product looks cheap because the window is behind it" points at a visible problem and invites a fix.

The second line is not louder. It is easier to place yourself inside.

## Give the first frame the same job as the first line

Words cannot carry an opening alone. If you say the photo looks cheap, show the flat photo. If you promise a faster way to pack lunch, show the overstuffed counter before you show the solution. A viewer should be able to understand the setup with the sound off.

This also keeps you honest. A dramatic line that has no matching image often signals a promise the video cannot keep. When the line and frame describe the same problem, the next beat becomes obvious: show the correction, the comparison, or the first step.

## Write options before you turn the camera on

The first acceptable sentence is rarely the best one. Draft a few openings for the same video, then read each aloud at the pace you would use on camera. Keep the line that does all of the following:

- identifies a real viewer or situation;
- can be understood on the first listen; and
- leads directly into proof you already have.

Cut anything that needs a second sentence to become interesting. Cut promises you would need to stretch the video to fulfill. The point is not to trap a random viewer for two seconds. It is to bring in someone who will care about the answer.

For example, a bookkeeping video might begin with "This is why your cash balance lies to you on Friday," then immediately show an invoice that has not been paid. The viewer knows the problem, and the video has somewhere to go.

## Test the handoff, not just the hook

A good hook can still lose people if the video starts over after it. Watch the first ten seconds as one unit. Does the next shot answer the opening question, or do you repeat the premise, introduce yourself, and finally begin?

Remove the second introduction. Put the useful visual earlier. If the hook names a mistake, show it before explaining why it happened. Those edits often matter more than finding a cleverer first sentence.

Keep a note of the comments and questions that appear under videos where people stayed. The phrases viewers use are usually better raw material than a polished topic label. They tell you what felt urgent enough to interrupt a scroll.

Treat the output as rough material. Say the contenders out loud, discard the ones that sound borrowed, and keep the one your video can deliver.

The aim is simple: let the first frame make a promise, then keep it without detouring. A short video earns attention one beat at a time. The opening is where that work begins.
